h1: The 6 Best Garden Augers of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 garden augers scored on diameter, length, drive fit and steel, from a 1.6 inch bulb bit to a 7 inch shrub auger.
summary: The MAXCCINO 4-Piece set is the auger to buy first: four sizes from 1.6 by 8.6 to 2.6 by 16.5 inches cover bulbs, plugs and bedding plants for under $25. If you only want one bit, the MAXCCINO 2 x 14.5 inch is the all-rounder. For shrubs and gallon pots, step up to the Power Planter 7 x 28 inch, but only with a strong drill. Match diameter to the plant before anything else.
intro: Most people buy an auger by length, and then stall the drill. Diameter does the real damage: the soil a bit has to lift grows with the square of its width, so a 4 inch auger asks far more of your drill than a 2 inch one of the same length. A drill that spins a bulb bit all afternoon can die in minutes on a shrub bit in clay.

We ranked six garden augers on the Primea framework, from a 1.6 inch bulb bit to a 7 inch extension model. Scores weigh diameter range, length, shank and drive style, steel construction and how well each suits the drills most owners have. Every pick here assumes a corded or 18V cordless drill with a clutch, held with both hands.

products.name: MAXCCINO 4-Piece Planting Auger Set
products.verdict: Four matched sizes on a 3/8 inch drive. One purchase covers bulbs, plugs and small perennials.
products.description:
MAXCCINO's set covers four sizes: 1.6 by 8.6, 3 by 12, 2 by 14.5 and 2.6 by 16.5 inches. Each uses a 3/8 inch non-slip drive and the seller suggests an 18V or higher drill. Cost stays in the under $25 bucket.

The set ranks first because a garden rarely needs just one hole. A 1.6 inch bit takes a bulb, the 3 inch bit takes a six-pack of annuals, and you do not stretch one auger to cover both. Against the single 2 x 14.5 below, you pay little extra for three additional sizes. The trade is quality: four thin bits are not built for rocky ground.

Buy it for a mixed bed and borders. The caveat is that nothing here digs deeper than 16.5 inches, so trees and posts need a bigger tool.
products.idealFor: Gardeners who move between bulbs, bedding plants and plugs.
products.skipIf: You are planting shrubs, trees or fence posts.

products.name: MAXCCINO 2 x 14.5 Inch Planting Auger
products.verdict: A 2 inch by 14.5 inch bit with extra blades on the shaft. The one auger most beds need.
products.description:
This MAXCCINO bit measures 2 inches across and 14.5 inches long, with a 3/8 inch non-slip drive and more blades along the shaft than a basic spiral. The suggested drill is 18V or higher, and the price sits in the under $25 bucket.

It ranks second since the same company sells a set that includes this exact 2 by 14.5 size, along with three others. Buy the single only if you are certain of the hole you need. The extra flighting helps lift soil out of the hole instead of packing it around the shaft, which is the common failure of cheap single-spiral bits.

The pick for bedding plants, small perennials and bulbs planted deep. The caveat is a fixed 2 inch width, which cannot take a gallon pot.
cons: The set offers more for the money
products.idealFor: Gardeners who want one all-round bit for bulbs and bedding plants.
products.skipIf: You would rather own the four-size set that includes this bit.

products.name: Power Planter DIY Guru 3 x 12 Inch Garden Auger
products.verdict: A 3 inch by 12 inch auger sold for dirt, clay, sand and rocky ground, and for mixing paint.
products.description:
Power Planter's DIY Guru is a 3 inch wide, 12 inch long auger that the maker lists for dirt, clay, sand and rocky soil. It also doubles as a mixing paddle for paint and cement, which no other pick here claims. The price sits in the $25 to $50 bucket.

It moves up from the 2 inch MAXCCINO because 3 inches takes a four-inch pot or a clump of crocus in one pass. At 12 inches it is shorter than the 14.5 and 16.5 inch bits, so the hole stops sooner. The listing does not state the drive size, so check the shank fits your chuck.

It suits a DIYer who wants hole-digging plus the odd mixing job. The caveat is depth: 12 inches is shallow for large bulbs.
pros: Listed for clay and rocky soil
products.idealFor: DIYers who want one bit for planting holes and light mixing jobs.
products.skipIf: You plant large bulbs that need holes deeper than 12 inches.

products.name: SYITCUN 4 x 16 Inch Heavy-Duty Auger
products.verdict: A 4 inch one-piece PCM steel auger. Big enough for shrubs and light post holes.
products.description:
SYITCUN's auger is 4 inches across and 16 inches long, built in one piece from PCM steel. That construction removes the welded joint where cheaper augers fail, and it costs under $25.

It ranks fourth because width brings a price in torque. A 4 inch bit in clay asks far more of the drill than the 2 inch MAXCCINO, so a strong cordless or a corded drill with a clutch matters. Against the Power Planter 7 inch, this one stays manageable for most drills, but it cannot take a gallon pot.

Pick it for transplants, shrubs and light post holes with a strong cordless drill. One gap: no shank or drive size is printed, so confirm the chuck fit with the seller before ordering.
products.idealFor: Gardeners planting shrubs, transplants and light post holes.
products.skipIf: You own a light drill or only plant bulbs.

products.name: Power Planter 7 x 28 Inch Extension Auger
products.verdict: A 7 inch by 28 inch auger with double 10-gauge flighting. For gallon pots and small trees.
products.description:
Power Planter's extension auger is the largest tool here: 7 inches across and 28 inches long, with a 1/2 inch non-slip hex drive and double 10-gauge flighting. The price falls in the $100 to $200 bucket, far above the rest of the ranking.

The heavy flighting is the reason to pay it. It clears a wide hole reliably, where thin spirals jam. But a 7 inch auger sets an enormous load on the drill, and the maker's own best-for note points to experienced DIYers with strong drills. It lands fifth because most gardeners do not need it.

Buy it for shrubs, gallon pots and small trees. The caveat is that a weak or cordless drill can stall it.
products.idealFor: Experienced DIYers who plant gallon pots, shrubs and small trees.
products.skipIf: You only plant bulbs, bedding plants or small perennials.

products.name: TCBWFY 1.6 x 16.5 Inch Planting Auger
products.verdict: A narrow 1.6 inch steel bit that goes 16.5 inches deep. Light on the drill, specific in use.
products.description:
TCBWFY makes a 1.6 inch wide, 16.5 inch long bit from heavy-duty steel with a black painted finish. The narrow width puts little load on a drill, and the length reaches deeper than most of the bits here. The price sits under $25.

It ranks last because it overlaps with the 1.6 by 8.6 inch bit inside the MAXCCINO set, which also adds three more sizes. The TCBWFY gives you only the deeper version. Its narrow shaft is also the least able to carry a wide plant plug.

A sound pick for deep, narrow bulb holes with a modest drill. Expect a missing drive size on the listing and a painted finish that will scuff in stony soil.
products.idealFor: Bulb planters who want a deep, narrow hole and a light load on the drill.
products.skipIf: You plant anything wider than a bulb or a small plug.

methodology.title: Diameter range
methodology.description: Hole width decides what you can plant. We compared bits from 1.6 to 7 inches against the plants each one suits.

methodology.title: Length and depth
methodology.description: Lengths run 12 to 28 inches. We scored whether depth suits the job the diameter implies.

methodology.title: Drive and drill fit
methodology.description: A 3/8 or 1/2 inch non-slip drive and the suggested drill size decide whether a typical cordless can run the bit.

methodology.title: Steel and construction
methodology.description: One-piece builds, flighting gauge and finish affect how a bit survives clay, roots and stone.

methodology.title: Versatility for the money
methodology.description: Sets, extra uses and the price bucket decided close calls between single bits.

whatMatters.detail: Diameter is the width of the hole, and it drives the load on your drill because the soil lifted grows with the square of the width. Bulbs need about 1.6 to 2 inches, plugs and annuals about 3, shrubs about 4 or more. Check the diameter in the title, then match it to the plant and the drill you own.

Length sets maximum hole depth, and the flighting must be long enough to lift soil up and out of that hole. Bits here run from 12 to 28 inches. Read the length on the listing, and remember that a deeper hole raises friction, so a long, narrow bit suits bulbs and a short, wide one suits transplants. Confirm the depth you need before you buy.

The shank must grip your chuck without slipping, which is why 3/8 and 1/2 inch non-slip drives matter. A hex shank resists spinning inside the chuck under load. Look for the drive size on the listing, and note the suggested voltage: an 18V cordless is the minimum for the MAXCCINO bits.

Flighting is the spiral that lifts soil, and its thickness decides whether it bends on a root or stone. One-piece steel avoids weld joints, and a gauge number such as 10 tells you the sheet thickness. Look for named steel, a gauge rating or a one-piece claim, not just the words heavy duty, because only the first three can be checked against a spec.

A set trades depth in each size for range, which suits mixed beds, while a single bit suits one repeated job. Check how many sizes are in the box and whether your most common hole is covered. The four-piece MAXCCINO spans 1.6 to 2.6 inch diameters, so it covers most beds, though it has no bit wide enough for a pot.

faq.q: What drill do I need for a garden auger?
faq.a: The MAXCCINO bits ask for an 18V or higher drill. The SYITCUN 4 inch and Power Planter 7 inch need more, ideally a corded or high-torque drill with a clutch, held with both hands to control kickback.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake?
faq.a: Using a wide bit on a weak drill. A 4 inch SYITCUN in clay stalls light cordless tools, and the user then blames the auger. Start narrow with the MAXCCINO set, and only step up in diameter when your drill handles it.

faq.q: Is the Power Planter 7 inch worth it over the SYITCUN?
faq.a: Only for gallon pots and small trees. The 7 x 28 inch costs far more, in the $100 to $200 bucket, and needs a strong drill. For shrubs and transplants the 4 x 16 inch SYITCUN is cheaper and more manageable.

faq.q: How do I use one safely?
faq.a: Wear gloves and eye protection, start at low speed with the tip on the planting spot, and let the flighting pull the bit down. Lift out soil frequently. If the drill grabs, release the trigger rather than fighting it.

faq.q: How do I maintain a garden auger?
faq.a: Brush off soil after each use and dry the bit, since steel rusts. The black paint on the TCBWFY will chip, so a light coat of oil on exposed steel helps. Check the shank for burrs that stop it seating in the chuck.

faq.q: Can I use an auger in rocky or root-filled soil?
faq.a: Use caution. The Power Planter DIY Guru is listed for rocky ground, but hitting a stone can twist the drill from your hands. Probe with a rod first, and switch to a hand tool when the bit hits resistance.

finalTake: The MAXCCINO 4-Piece set is the best first auger because it spans bulbs, plugs and bedding plants for under $25. Choose the single 2 x 14.5 if you only dig one size, the SYITCUN for shrubs and the Power Planter 7 x 28 inch for gallon pots and small trees. Always size the bit to your drill, not just the plant.
